Counter-culture. The social, artistic, and political movements of the nineteen sixties and nineteen seventies that rejected dominant cultural values, institutional authority, and conformity. Rooted partly in the Beat generation's literary rebellion of the nineteen fifties, counter-culture became a mass movement encompassing music, visual art, literature, and lifestyle.

Counter-culture emerged in the early nineteen sixties among college students and urban intellectuals, accelerated by the Vietnam War and civil rights conflicts. Generational rupture was both artistic and political. Central preoccupations included personal liberation, psychedelic experience, rejection of materialism, and experimental artistic forms. Writers explored consciousness expansion through both chemical and textual means.

The Beats pioneered the literary aesthetic—spontaneous composition, oral performance, explicit content—that counter-culture amplified and popularized. The audience grew exponentially from underground to mass phenomenon. Music, especially rock and folk, became the primary vehicle of counter-cultural expression and political messaging. Artists like Dylan transformed folk ballads into protest, while rock bands articulated generational alienation.

Counter-culture challenged taboos around sexuality, drug use, gender roles, and family structure, proposing alternative communities and ways of living. Communal experiments and new social arrangements were both utopian aspiration and lived reality. By the mid-nineteen seventies, counter-culture either became commercialized or retreated. Its political aspirations largely failed, but its artistic legacy endured. Consumerism co-opted rebellion, yet the challenge to cultural norms persisted. The movement generated canonical literary figures like Norman Mailer and Susan Sontag, as established writers responded to revolutionary fervor.
